messages.content:
You are a helpful writing assistant. You help professionals draft clear,
effective workplace communication.

I have to tell my manager I'm going to miss the Friday deadline on the
migration. It's my fault - I underestimated it. I want to say it straight
without it turning into a whole thing. Can you help me word it?

Here are a few options, from most concise to slightly more detailed. Pick the one that best matches your manager's communication style and your workplace culture.

**Option 1 (Direct & solution-focused)**
> Hi [Name], I need to let you know I won't meet Friday's migration deadline. I underestimated the scope and need a few more days to complete it properly. I'm on track to finish by [new date] and will keep you updated on progress. I take full responsibility for the delay and will adjust my planning to avoid this going forward. Let me know if this impacts any other priorities I should be aware of.

**Option 2 (Shorter)**
> Hi [Name], I'm going to miss Friday's migration deadline. I underestimated the work required and need until [new date] to finish it properly. I'll keep you posted on my progress and will make sure my timelines are realistic going forward. Please let me know if you need to adjust any downstream plans in the meantime.

**Option 3 (If dependencies/impact are a concern)**
> Hi [Name], I won't be able to hit Friday's migration deadline. I underestimated the complexity and need until [new date] to complete it without cutting corners. I've already flagged any teams or tasks that might be affected and am working to minimize the ripple. I take full responsibility for the delay and will improve my estimation process for future work. Happy to sync briefly if you want to adjust priorities or timeline expectations.

**Why these work:**
- They state the issue upfront without padding or hedging
- Take clear ownership ("I underestimated") without self-flagellation
- Give a concrete new timeline
- Focus on next steps and impact management rather than dwelling on the mistake
- Leave the door open for course correction without forcing a meeting

**Delivery tips to keep it from "turning into a whole thing":**
- Send it **as soon as possible** (don't wait until Friday morning)
- Stick to **one message**. Don't follow up with extra explanations unless specifically asked
- If they want to discuss it, be ready with: what's actually blocking you, how you're solving it, and what's working vs. what's not
- Keep your tone matter-of-fact, not defensive or overly apologetic

**What to avoid:**
- Over-apologizing or dramatic language ("I completely dropped the ball…")
- Explaining every technical detail or edge case
- Blaming tools, vague requirements, or others unless they're genuinely the root cause
- Adding "just wanted to give a heads up" framing (it's already past the heads-up stage)

Want me to adjust the tone, add specific dates/dependencies, or match your manager's preferred communication style? I can fine-tune it.
